name: composed-method
intent: Divide the work into methods that each perform one identifiable task, written as a short outline of invocations in which every operation sits at the same level of abstraction, so a reader grasps the task top-down and every change lands on one small, named step.
problem: A method accumulates several concerns at once: high-level policy ('validate the order, then charge it') interleaved with low-level detail (a loop index, a string concatenation, a counter), so the method grows long, needs comments to mark its sections, and changes for more than one reason. Readers must simulate the whole body to learn what it does, duplication hides inside similar-looking blocks, and anyone who must change one decision - a subclass in particular - ends up copying the method and editing it.
context: Applies wherever code is decomposed into named routines and is read far more often than written: long-lived domain and application code, code review and onboarding, framework base classes that must expose override hooks, and code whose steps carry contracts worth testing separately. It is a source-level discipline rather than a runtime structure, so a language needs only routines and some notion of non-public helpers; it matters most exactly where methods have grown past the point a reader can hold them in mind.
benefits: The outline communicates intent: a reviewer or caller learns what the method does from a handful of names instead of simulating the body, and descends into low-level detail only when it is relevant.
Changes become local: fixing a bug, tuning a rule or adding a branch touches one small step, which is Beck's point that small methods let you 'isolate assumptions'.
Duplication surfaces early: the same block appearing in three methods becomes one named step, so the bottom-up use of the pattern pays for itself immediately.

Inheritance and extension get real hooks: each step can be overridden or replaced individually, so a subclass changes one decision instead of duplicating the whole method (Coulman's ComposedMethod and inheritance argument).

Behaviour becomes testable at the level at which it is described: the outline tests the whole task, and a step that carries its own contract (parsing, rounding, validation) is a legitimate unit of its own.

The naming pressure is diagnostic: a fragment that cannot be given an honest name is doing more than one thing, or belongs to a concept that has not been extracted yet - the code improves because the vocabulary is forced.
Reviews and diffs stay readable: the outline is stable while a step changes, so a change is visible as a change of one intention rather than a body edit in a long method.
tradeoffs: Naming is the new cost: every extraction needs a name truer than the code it replaces, and a helper whose name only restates its one-line body adds a jump without adding information.

More parts, more indirection: control flow now leaves the method, so readers chase steps and debuggers jump across the file; Beck's own caveat is that novices 'can't figure out where any real work is getting done'.

Mechanical extraction can go wrong: a step cut where a comment happened to be (rather than where the abstraction changes) breaks the symmetry of the outline, and steps that must exchange several locals push parameter lists up - the point where Method Object or Parameter Object is the real fix.
Extracted steps that write fields or globals instead of exchanging values turn the outline's order into an unstated temporal contract, so the class becomes harder to reason about than before.

Call overhead is small but not free, and a hot inner loop can notice it; the remedy is to inline deliberately (Inline Method) rather than to keep a method for symmetry - and never to argue about it without measurement.
Over-application produces dozens of one-line helpers and classes with no cohesion; at that point the helpers are telling you to Extract Class, not to extract more methods.
In languages where privacy is convention rather than enforcement, non-public steps are still reachable by tests, subclasses and same-package code, which freezes internals the outline meant to hide.

participants.responsibility: Performs one identifiable task; its body is a short sequence of invocations of the next level down and contains no operation that belongs to a lower level of abstraction.

Implements exactly one of those invocations, named with an intention-revealing selector, non-public to the rest of the system, and taking its state as parameters and return values rather than through shared mutable fields.
Reads the outline as a summary of the task and descends only into the step in question; the same steps are the hooks a subclass replaces instead of copying the method.

use_cases: Long methods built up over time whose sections are marked by comments: each comment becomes a step name and the method becomes an outline.
A method with several responsibilities (validate, compute, persist) that must change independently and be reviewed one concern at a time.
Framework or library base classes that must offer override points: each step becomes a documented extension point, usually combined with Template Method or NVI.
Top-down design of an algorithm: write the outline first, with steps as not-yet-implemented calls, and fill them in one at a time.
Bottom-up refactoring when the same block appears in several methods: extract it as a named step and call it from each outline.
Making behaviour testable in isolation: steps with their own contracts (parsing input, rounding money, validating rules) become separately testable units.
TDD workflow: write the test for the composed method outline first, asserting each step in sequence, then implement each step as a separate testable unit.
Complex business rules that combine multiple conditional branches: decompose each branch condition and its body into a clearly named step, making the rule engine visible and auditable.
Command or handler objects that orchestrate a multi-step process (validate request, authorize caller, execute operation, emit event, log outcome): each phase is a named step in the composed method.

Production Rails code: Basecamp's Event::Relaying#relay_now reads as an outline of named steps (relay_to_or_revoke_from_timeline, relay_to_webhooks_later), each descending into its own relayer class - the 'fractal' consistency of composed methods in a shipped product, documented by 37signals.

Acceptance and integration test suites: each scenario is written as a composed method at a single level of abstraction (sign_in, create_todo, mark_complete), delegating the mechanics to named helpers or page objects so the test tells the user-level story.

JUnit 4's refactored internals: Beck documents TestCase together with the RunAfter, ExpectException and FailedTest method objects as chained composed outlines, each invocation staying at one level of abstraction (his 'Nested Method Object' evolution of the pattern).
avoid_when: The method already does one thing in a few lines: extraction yields a helper whose name restates its body - leave it, and if anything apply Inline Method.
The method is a pure data transformation: a map/filter/reduce chain or comprehension states the stages more directly (Collection Pipeline, Function Composition).
The units you want need the same half-dozen locals: introduce a Parameter Object or turn the invocation into a Method Object or a new class before threading parameters through an outline.
A hot inner loop where call overhead has been measured and matters: keep the code together and buy readability elsewhere.
Throwaway code (a spike, a one-off script) that no one will revisit: the navigation cost exceeds any benefit there.
anti_patterns: Mechanical extraction: one-line private methods that merely restate their name (`doWork()` calling `stepOne()`), producing a debugger pinball machine without added meaning.

Level violation: the outline mixes policy-level steps with raw detail (a loop index, string concatenation, a log call), so extraction increased the method count while breaking the same-level-of-abstraction rule.
State-passing through the object: extracted steps assign fields or globals and later steps read them, making the order of the outline a hidden contract and destroying independent testability.
Using extraction to make a god class look tidy: hundreds of private helpers on one class instead of extracting the concepts they belong to.
Publishing the steps: making helpers public or protected for tests, same-package callers or speculative reuse freezes implementation details and turns the outline into an API.
Comment-driven boundaries: splitting where a comment happened to sit rather than where the abstraction changes, producing asymmetric outlines that mix levels again.

Same-name coupling: the outline method and its primary step share a root word (e.g., `replace()` calls `replaceAll()`), suggesting the step name only restates the caller rather than describing a distinct abstraction - Esko Luontola's critique of 'One Thing: Extract Till You Drop'.
Parameter tsunami: extracting steps that each need the same 6+ parameters, passed as a long call chain; the fix is a Parameter Object or Method Object, not more extraction.
False cohesion in steps: extracting a method named `process()` that itself contains multiple concerns at different levels - the extraction adds a hop without fixing the underlying level violation.
design_principles: Single responsibility: one identifiable task per routine; a step that resists an honest name is doing more than one thing.
Single level of abstraction (SLAP): all operations inside a method belong to the same conceptual level, so the reader never changes altitude within a method.
Information hiding: the steps are non-public; the outline is the callable contract and the way the task is achieved stays inside.
Separation of concerns: policy and flow are separated from detail, which is what makes the detail independently reviewable, testable and replaceable.
DRY: the bottom-up application turns duplicated fragments into one named step - the single place where the next bug is fixed.
Open/closed through small hooks: the outline stays closed for modification while subclasses and callers extend behaviour by replacing individual steps.
best_practices: Name steps after their effect (intention-revealing selectors); a step you cannot name without 'and' is two steps or the wrong boundary.
Keep the outline's invocations at one consistent level: when the next level is needed, descend into a step instead of adding detail to the outline.
Use top-down composition while designing and bottom-up extraction while maintaining - they are complementary, not alternatives.
Keep steps non-public and pass data in and out rather than sharing mutable state, so the order of the outline is not a contract.
Make helpers static or free where they need no state: they cannot accidentally couple to the object and are easier to test.
Stop when names stop adding information, and follow clusters of helpers that share data into a new class (Extract Class) or a Method Object.
Test through the outline; give a step its own tests only when it has a contract of its own (parsing, rounding, validation rules).
Write the outline first, with step calls as not-yet-implemented stubs, then fill in each step - this forces clear thinking about the task decomposition before details distract.

Apply the 'extract till you drop' heuristic: if you can extract another method from a step, the step is doing more than one thing and should be split (Robert C. Martin, 'One Thing: Extract Till You Drop', 2009).
When a step's parameter list grows beyond 4-5 parameters, consider introducing a Parameter Object or extracting a new class rather than threading loose parameters through the outline.
Use blank lines as a smell signal: a blank line between two statements often indicates a missing abstraction boundary - the block after the blank line should likely be a named step.
sources: Kent Beck, Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns (Prentice Hall, 1997) - Composed Method (pp. 21-22): divide a program into methods that perform one identifiable task, and keep all operations in a method at the same level of abstraction.
Kent Beck, Implementation Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 2007) - Composed Method: methods call out to other methods, each of which are roughly the same level of abstraction.
Kent Beck, 'Two More Implementation Patterns' (originally published 2007, newsletter 2023) - Nested Method Object and Conditional Factory patterns extend Composed Method for JUnit 4 refactoring.
Linda Rising, Patterns Almanac entry for Beck 1997 (Composed Method, pages 21-22): https://smallmemory.charlesweir.com/almanac/almanac/Beck97.html

Jorge Manrubia, 'The Composed Method implementation pattern' (2009) - detailed treatment of cohesion, clear interfaces, and symmetry as the three fundamental properties ruling method design: https://www.jorgemanrubia.com/2009/06/28/the-composed-method-implementation-pattern/
Robert C. Martin, Clean Code (Prentice Hall, 2008) - Functions should descend only one level of abstraction (Chapter 3), the SLAP principle applied at scale.

David Bernstein, 'The Single Level of Abstraction Principle' (DZone, 2016) - explains how mixing abstraction levels increases software viscosity and why keeping methods at one level makes code more testable, extendable, and understandable.

Principles Wiki, 'Single Level of Abstraction (SLA)' - formally defines SLA and its relationship to Extract Method, Extract Class, cohesion, and mental grouping: http://principles-wiki.net/principles:single_level_of_abstraction

Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob), 'One Thing: Extract Till You Drop' (2009) - demonstrates progressive extraction of a method to the point where no further extraction is possible, arguing that 'extract till you can't extract anymore' is the correct heuristic for 'one thing'.

Esko Luontola, comment on 'One Thing: Extract Till You Drop' (2009) - adds that all operations in a method should be at a lower level of abstraction than the name of the method, and that 'replace' and 'replaceAllSymbols' are at the same level.

Itay Maman, comment on 'One Thing: Extract Till You Drop' (2009) - warns of two critical over-extraction issues: the time cost of extraction and the loss of encapsulation when private methods become effectively public through subclassing.

related_patterns_notes.macro-method: Macro-method expresses a composite behaviour by sequencing method calls; composed-method is the stricter discipline requiring same-level-of-abstraction steps.
related_patterns_notes.method-object: Method Object turns a complex method into an object so its locals become fields, enabling further simplification; Kent Beck's 'Nested Method Object' (2007/2023) chains method objects as an evolution of composed method for JUnit 4.
related_patterns_notes.template-method: Template Method defines an algorithm skeleton in a base class and lets subclasses override individual steps; composed-method provides the step granularity that makes template method override points intention-revealing.
related_patterns_notes.nvi: Non-Virtual Interface (NVI) wraps a virtual method in a non-virtual 'template' that enforces pre/post conditions; the template is a natural composed-method outline whose steps are the override hooks.
related_patterns_notes.collecting-parameter: Collecting Parameter passes a container into a method so multiple steps can accumulate results into it; a composed-method outline can use a collecting parameter as one of its step inputs/outputs.
related_patterns_notes.intention-revealing-interface: Both patterns share the goal of making code self-documenting through names; composed-method applies this at the method level, while intention-revealing interface applies it at the class level.
related_patterns_notes.function-composition: Function composition chains pure functions in pipelines; composed-method achieves a similar declarative effect within an imperative method, with the additional constraint that steps share no mutable state.
related_patterns_notes.chain-of-responsibility: Chain of Responsibility chains handler objects where each may handle or delegate; a composed-method outline with conditional step delegation resembles a hand-written chain, without the object-allocation overhead.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy encapsulates a family of algorithms behind a common interface; each composed-method step can delegate to a Strategy, keeping the outline at policy level while the algorithm detail lives in the Strategy object.
related_patterns_notes.decorator: Kent Beck notes that Nested Method Object chains can be viewed as Decorators - each Link decorates the next with additional behaviour (timeout, exception handling); the outline remains the composition contract.
